request_debug.prompt_preview:
You write per-candidate post-mortems for a slopmortem pipeline. Given a fresh pitch and one dead-startup canonical document, produce a single LLMSynthesis JSON object that explains why this dead startup is similar, where the new pitch could diverge, what killed the dead startup, and what the new founder should learn.

Rules:
- Ground every claim in the candidate document or in tool calls. Do not invent facts.
- A `Trusted facts` block (typed pipeline data — not user input) appears below the pitc

response.text: {"candidate_id":"vine::social_communication","name":"vine","one_liner":"Twitter-owned short-form 6-second looping video platform shut down in 2017 after losing creators and ad revenue to Instagram, YouTube, and Snapchat.","similarity":{"business_model":{"score":1,"rationale":"Vine was a free, ad-supported consumer video platform (ad_revenue, free price point). The new pitch is a B2C marketplace charging a 20% transaction fee on paid 1:1 video consults. These are fundamentally different monetization architectures — broadcast/passive vs. transactional/interactive."},"market":{"score":2,"rationale":"Both involve video and influencers/creators in a consumer context, and Vine explicitly contributed to the rise of influencers. However, Vine was a global mass-market short-form content platform; the new pitch targets a niche geographic market (Tokyo and Seoul) focused on beauty verticals with a paid consultation model. The overlap is superficial."},"gtm":{"score":1,"rationale":"Vine grew via viral social sharing, Twitter distribution, and organic user-generated content loops. The new pitch would need to onboard specific beauty influencers in two cities and match them with paying fans — a supply-side curated GTM with direct sales, not viral distribution."},"stage_scale":{"score":3,"rationale":"Both are early-stage consumer products targeting a creator/fan dynamic. Vine reached 200M users at scale; the new pitch is geographically constrained and niche. Some structural similarity in needing a critical mass of creators before consumer utility kicks in."}},"why_similar":"Both products sit at the intersection of influencers and consumer video engagement. Vine pioneered the creator economy dynamic — influencers building audiences who consume their content — which is the upstream relationship the new pitch seeks to monetize. Both are consumer-facing, mobile-first, and dependent on a supply side of creators agreeing to participate on the platform before demand-side fans get value.","where_diverged":"Multiple concrete dimensions diverge: (1) Monetization — Vine relied on ad_revenue with a free product; the new pitch charges a 20% transaction fee on paid 1:1 consults. (2) Interaction model — Vine was passive broadcast (6-second public clips); the new pitch is private, synchronous, paid 1:1 video consultation. (3) Geography — Vine was global; the new pitch is explicitly scoped to Tokyo and Seoul. (4) Vertical — Vine was horizontal entertainment/comedy/music; the new pitch is beauty-specific. (5) Customer relationship — Vine had no direct fan-to-creator payment; the new pitch is built entirely on that transaction.","failure_causes":["creator exodus to competing platforms (Instagram, YouTube, Snapchat)","no direct monetization for creators — no revenue sharing or payment tools","advertiser and marketer abandonment of the platform","Twitter parent company strategic neglect and eventual shutdown decision","inability to differentiate from feature-copying incumbents (Instagram Video, Snapchat)","lack of creator retention mechanisms as platform matured"],"lessons_for_input":["Build direct creator monetization into the product from day one — do not rely on ad revenue that can disappear with platform owner decisions.","Design strong creator lock-in by making the consultation history, fan relationships, and earnings data non-portable to competing platforms.","Validate that target influencers in Tokyo and Seoul will actually accept paid consult requests before investing in consumer-side growth.","Keep the geographic scope tight initially so you can deliver a high-quality supply of bookable influencers rather than spreading thin globally.","Ensure your transaction-fee model covers influencer payout rates that are competitive enough to prevent them from routing fans off-platform via DMs or other channels."]}
